title: Discrete Fourier Transform
body:
The version a computer can actually run. A [[Fourier Transform]] wants a continuous function and an
integral over all of $\mathbb{R}$; a machine has $N$ numbers in an array. Replace the integral with
a finite sum and you get

$$
X_k = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_n\,e^{-2\pi i k n / N}, \qquad k = 0, 1, \dots, N-1
$$

with the inverse differing only by the sign in the exponent and a factor of $1/N$. Input: $N$
samples of a signal. Output: $N$ complex numbers, where $|X_k|$ is the amplitude of the $k$th
frequency and $\arg X_k$ is its phase. **$N$ numbers in, $N$ numbers out**, so nothing is lost and
nothing is invented; it is a change of basis, not a compression.

## It is a matrix

Write $\omega = e^{-2\pi i / N}$, a primitive $N$th root of unity (see [[Roots of Unity]]). Then
$X = F x$ where $F$ is the **DFT matrix**, $F_{kn} = \omega^{kn}$:

$$
F = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\
1 & \omega & \omega^2 & \cdots & \omega^{N-1} \\
1 & \omega^2 & \omega^4 & \cdots & \omega^{2(N-1)} \\
\vdots & & & & \vdots \\
1 & \omega^{N-1} & \omega^{2(N-1)} & \cdots & \omega^{(N-1)^2}
\end{pmatrix}
$$

So the transform is [[Matrix Multiplication]], which is why this course lands in linear algebra
territory. The rows of $F$ are orthogonal and $\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}F$ is unitary, so the rows form an
[[Orthonormal Basis]] of $\mathbb{C}^N$ and **the inverse transform is just the conjugate
transpose**. That is the discrete echo of the orthogonality argument in
[[Fourier Coefficients]]: same [[Projection]], finite sum instead of an integral.

| | Continuous ([[Fourier Series]]) | Discrete (here) |
|---|---|---|
| Basis | $\{e^{inx}\}$, infinitely many | $N$ rows of $F$ |
| Coefficient | $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int f e^{-inx}dx$ | $\sum_n x_n \omega^{kn}$ |
| Orthogonality by | integral over a period | sum over $N$ roots of unity |
| Recovers | a function | the original $N$ samples exactly |

## Facts worth holding

- **The naive computation is $O(N^2)$**: $N$ outputs, each a sum of $N$ terms. That is a dense
  matrix-vector product, and it is what makes the [[Fast Fourier Transform]] worth having.
- The samples are assumed **periodic**, because the transform only knows the $N$ values it was
  given. If the signal does not repeat cleanly across the window, the implied jump at the wrap-around
  point spreads energy across every bin. That is spectral leakage, and it is
  [[Gibbs Phenomenon]]'s discrete cousin.
- Bin $k$ corresponds to frequency $k f_s / N$. Bins above $N/2$ are the negative frequencies, and
  for real input $X_{N-k} = \overline{X_k}$, so half the output is redundant. The fold at $N/2$ is
  the Nyquist frequency of [[Sampling Theorem]].
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] (MATH 2303) introduces this as a change of basis on data and
  hands the transform itself here, the same introduces-then-owns split as Calc 2 to Calc 3.
  [[Wavelet Transform]] is the alternative basis that trades frequency precision for time
  localisation.
